caption:
A refund feels good until you realize what it actually is.

You overpaid all year. The government held your money and gave it back with zero interest.

And just so we are clear, if you owed CRA anything, they already took it before that refund hit your account. So what you received is what is left after they helped themselves.

Here is what I would actually do with whatever is left.

If your June instalment is coming up, put it there first. That deadline sneaks up on people every single year.

Beyond that, it really comes down to your strategy. RRSP, TFSA, and FHSA are all solid options depending on your situation and goals. None of them is automatically the right answer. 

If you have existing debt, check the interest rate before you throw money at it. Pay down the highest rate first. Your line of credit at 8% is a very different conversation than your mortgage at 3%.

We personally plan for a small refund every year on purpose. Mostly because we put it toward our half cow order and it genuinely saves us a fortune on groceries. Highly recommend both the tax strategy and the beef (right @longrunranching? 😉😉).

caption:
Here is what “I’ll just write it off” actually does.

In Alberta, a small business pays about 11 percent corporate tax. So you buy a $10,000 thing to write it off, and it lowers your tax by about $1,100.

You spent ten thousand dollars to save eleven hundred. You are still out $8,900.

A write off is not a coupon. It does not hand you the money back, it just means you do not pay tax on that part. Buying something you do not actually need to save 11 cents on the dollar is not a strategy.

Now, if you needed the thing anyway, buy it and claim it. That is different. The trap is buying it just to save tax.

One thing I’ve learned running a firm and advising business owners is that compensation decisions are rarely just about the numbers.

Yes, tax matters. But so does how something feels on the receiving end.

A gift can be thoughtful, personal, and meaningful. It can also feel awkward if it shows up on a pay stub later and no one expected it. That disconnect is usually where frustration comes from, not the tax itself.

Ever wonder what to do when your phone is both your office and your lifeline to friends and family? 

Here’s the deal: if you’re using one phone for business and personal, it’s common to expense half the cost. Fifty percent is usually the sweet spot I recommend... not too much, not too little.

But what if your corporation buys the phone outright? Well, now it’s a business asset. 

That means when you eventually sell or trade it in, you’ll need to show that on your books too. It’s not just a one-and-done expense.

Bottom line: mixed-use phones are normal, but the way you handle the cost matters. Keep it simple, keep it fair, and your accountant (and future self) will thank you.

caption:
If you are self-employed, November is the PERFECT time to get organized before tax season sneaks up!

No, you do not need to do everything at once. 

But you should start here:

1. Get your receipts organized.
Pull everything together, total it up, and make a summary for the year.
This will make tax prep simple and save you hours later.

2. List your major purchases.
Write down anything big you bought this year for your business.
Items like laptops, tools, or office furniture matter for deductions.

3. Review last year’s tax slips.
Look at what you received before, like RRSP contributions, childcare, or tuition.
Make a checklist so you know exactly what to expect this year.

4. Track your mileage.
If you have not been doing it all year, total it now.
Use an app or simple spreadsheet to record business versus personal travel.

5. Separate your accounts.
If you are still mixing personal and business, open a separate account for 2026.
It will make your bookkeeping cleaner and less stressful. (hint - same goes for the credit card!)

6. Check your instalments.
If you make instalment payments, confirm they are up to date.
If you have not been paying them, set funds aside now so spring is easier.

You do not need perfection. You just need to START!

I promise this small effort now will make next year feel lighter and more organized, for both you and your accountant!

caption:
If you own a corporation with a December year-end, this is your reminder to get organized before December sneaks up.

You don’t need to overcomplicate it. Just start with these:

1. Catch up your bookkeeping: Go through your books and make sure everything is reconciled to your bank statements.

2. Review your 2026 pay structure: Decide how you plan to pay yourself next year - salary, dividends, or a mix of both. Getting ahead now helps you plan your taxes and cash flow with confidence.

3. Build a budget: Start planning for 2026 now. Look at what worked this year, what changed, and what needs more attention.

4. Check your instalments: Make sure they are up to date and paid. If you have a profit, plan for what is coming soon. If you don’t know, talk to your accountant and plan ahead.

5. Confirm payroll remittances: Double-check that all months are filed and paid. It’s one of the easiest things to miss and the simplest to fix now.

In plain terms, this is the prep work that keeps your accountant happy and your year end smooth.

If you have fallen behind, the best step is to get caught up as quickly as possible. The longer you wait, the bigger the bill grows and the harder it is to dig out.

I have helped many business owners get caught up, and I do it without judgment.

caption:
Here is what you actually need to know if you own a corporation in Canada.

How you pay yourself, whether through salary, dividends, or a mix of both, affects much more than just your tax bill. It changes your cash flow, CPP contributions, RRSP room, and even how lenders view your income when you apply for financing.

Let’s break it down in simple terms:

Salary: Creates RRSP room and contributes to CPP. It gives you a steady income for personal budgeting and can make borrowing easier. It also means consistent payroll costs for the company and source deductions to remit.

Dividends: Come from corporate profits after tax. They provide flexibility in how and when you withdraw funds but do not reduce corporate taxable income. They also do not create RRSP room or CPP contributions, which can matter for long term planning.

Bonus: Usually used strategically near year end to reduce corporate income when profits are higher than expected. It is a short term tool, not an ongoing pay structure.

Where most business owners go wrong is leaving this decision to the last minute. By then, you are reacting to your numbers instead of leading them.

A strong CFO plan looks at your full picture before year end. It blends salary, dividends, and bonuses to balance personal and corporate taxes while keeping cash flow healthy.

The goal is not just to save tax once. It is to build a structure that keeps your business stable and your personal finances predictable year after year.

If you have not reviewed your pay structure this quarter, this is your reminder to do it now.

It is one of the simplest ways to build confidence and clarity before December.
